templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: Many species of cone snail, a group of venomous marine predators, capture prey by striking single animals with a harpoon-like tooth. Conus geographus and Conus tulipa, by contrast, engulf entire schools of small fish with a distensible, net-like mouth. In the venoms of these two species, Helena Safavi-Hemami and colleagues identified a form of insulin closely resembling that of fish, which impairs the swimming of fish exposed to it in the water. Fish insulin was absent, however, from the venoms of five fish-eating cone snails that hunt with a harpoon and from those of snails that prey on worms or mollusks.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the fish-like insulin found in some cone snail venoms?
options: It is likely injected into each fish through the harpoon-like tooth that cone snails use to strike prey.
It likely gives fish-eating cone snails as a group an edge over cone snails that prey on worms or mollusks.
Whether a snail’s venom contains it likely depends more on how the snail captures its prey than on what that prey is.
It likely resembles fish insulin because the snails absorb it from the fish they eat instead of making it.
items.explanation: The text describes two groups of cone snails that both eat fish: the two species that engulf groups of fish with a net-like mouth, whose venoms contain the fish-like insulin, and five species that strike fish with a harpoon, whose venoms do not. Since both groups eat fish but only one has the insulin, its presence seems to follow the way a snail hunts rather than the kind of prey it eats.

A.why_wrong: The text says the insulin affects fish exposed to it in the water, and it was found only in the two species that engulf fish, not in the snails that strike with a harpoon.

B.why_wrong: The insulin is not a trait of fish-eating cone snails as a group: the five fish-eaters that hunt with a harpoon lack it.

D.recipe: plausible but unsupported, ruled out by a stated fact
D.why_wrong: If the snails simply took in insulin from the fish they eat, the five fish-eating harpoon hunters would have it too, but the team found none in their venoms.

sources.what: Sci.News on Safavi-Hemami et al., PNAS 2015: Conus geographus and C. tulipa use the same fish-trapping method (venom released into the water, stretchy mouth-like part aimed at fish); one venom insulin very similar to fish insulin; synthetic version lowered zebrafish blood glucose and disrupted swimming of fish exposed through the water; no fish insulin in the venom of five fish-eating ambush (harpoon) cone snails, nor in snails that prey on mollusks or worms

items.notes: Natural science (venom biology). Premise 1: the net-hunting fish-eaters have the insulin. Premise 2: harpoon-hunting fish-eaters (and worm and mollusk hunters) lack it. Unstated conclusion: the insulin goes with the net-hunting method, not with a fish diet. B and D are each killed by the harpoon fish-eaters clause; A by the water exposure and by where the insulin was found.

band7.why: Planned band 6 (wave-2 plan sets every Central Ideas hard cell to 6). Two premises (net hunters have the insulin; harpoon fish-eaters and worm and mollusk hunters lack it) and one unstated link (hunting method, not diet, tracks it); key paraphrased; distractors TWI (harpoon delivery), CON-half (fish-eaters as a group), UNS mechanism (absorbed from prey), B and D partly right but both fall to the harpoon fish-eater clause the key itself needs. Options 18 to 22 words, no stance word or aside, so strong band 6.

items.passage: Court reporters must be certified as transcribing speech with at least 95 percent accuracy, a certification based predominantly on the speech of lawyers and judges. Linguist Taylor Jones and colleagues asked 27 reporters employed in Philadelphia’s courts to transcribe recordings of speakers of African American English (AAE), a dialect governed by its own consistent grammatical rules. Although the recordings were played clearly and more loudly than courtroom testimony typically is, only 59.5 percent of the transcribed sentences were accurate, and no reporter achieved 95 percent accuracy.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the reporters’ errors in the study?
options: They likely reflect a gap between the speech the reporters’ certification covers and the speech they were asked to transcribe.
They were likely more frequent than the errors the reporters would make when transcribing AAE speakers testifying in court.
They likely show that the reporters’ certification overstates their accuracy with the speech of lawyers and judges.
They likely arose because AAE lacks the regular grammatical patterns that reporters depend on when they transcribe speech.
items.explanation: The reporters had all been certified at 95 percent accuracy on a test based mainly on the speech of lawyers and judges, yet with AAE they reached only 59.5 percent, even though the recordings were clear and louder than courtroom testimony. Since poor listening conditions are ruled out, the errors most likely come from the difference between the speech their certification measures and the AAE speech in the study.

B.why_wrong: The recordings were played more clearly and loudly than courtroom testimony usually is, so in court the reporters would likely make at least as many errors, not fewer.

C.why_wrong: The study tested only recordings of AAE speakers, so its results say nothing about how accurately the reporters transcribe lawyers and judges, the speech their certification is based on.

D.why_wrong: The text describes AAE as a dialect with its own consistent grammatical rules, so the errors cannot be blamed on a lack of regular patterns.

sources.what: Language Magazine (2019) on Jones, Kalbfeld, Hancock and Clark, Testifying While Black (Language 95:2): 27 court stenographers in the Philadelphia courts; transcriptionists required to be certified at 95% accuracy, certifications based primarily on the speech of lawyers and judges; recordings played clearly and louder than in court; only 59.5% of transcribed sentences accurate; none performed at 95% accuracy; reporters both white and black whose trainings did not match their tasks

items.notes: Social science (linguistics and law). Premise 1: certification is based mainly on lawyers' and judges' speech. Premise 2: with clear, loud AAE recordings the certified reporters fell far below 95 percent. Conclusion (the source's own: trainings did not match their tasks): the shortfall comes from the kind of speech, not from hearing conditions. Review: the state is no longer named as setting the requirement (the source says only that all transcriptionists must be certified at 95 percent); B now needs a step (court is harder to hear, so errors there would not be fewer) instead of contradicting the volume clause outright; C is a true premise with a wrong conclusion; D is the misconception the rules gloss refutes.

fixes: passage: “Pennsylvania requires court reporters to be certified” became “Court reporters must be certified” (Language Magazine: all transcriptionists are required to be certified at 95 percent; no state rule named)

hardened to a fair band 6: B (recordings harder to hear) contradicted the volume clause outright; now it claims the study errors outnumber those the reporters would make in court, which needs the clause turned around

band7.why: Planned band 6, after hardening. Key needs two links (clear, loud recordings rule out hearing; certification rests on other speech, so the shortfall is a coverage gap); B now needs the volume clause turned around, C is a true premise with a wrong conclusion, D the misconception the rules gloss refutes. Options 17 to 20 words, no stance word, so band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1869 novel Oldtown Folks.

Every New England village, if you only think of it, must have its do-nothing as regularly as it has its school-house or meeting-house. Nature is always wide awake in the matter of compensation. Work, thrift, and industry are such an incessant steam-power in Yankee life, that society would burn itself out with intense friction were there not interposed here and there the lubricating power of a decided do-nothing,—a man who won’t be hurried, and won’t work, and will take his ease in his own way, in spite of the whole protest of his neighborhood to the contrary.
items.stem: Based on the text, what does the narrator most likely believe about a village’s do-nothing?
options: He causes the friction that troubles a village whose members resent his refusal to work.
He offers his hardworking neighbors an example of the idleness they must avoid if their village is to thrive.
He is an embarrassment that a village tolerates until his neighbors persuade him to change.
He serves as a counterweight that keeps a tireless community from wearing itself out.
items.explanation: The narrator says that Yankee work, thrift, and industry run like a steam engine so hard that society would “burn itself out with intense friction” without the “lubricating power” of a do-nothing. Like oil in a machine, the do-nothing eases the strain of all that activity, so the narrator sees him as a useful balance to a community that would otherwise exhaust itself.

A.why_wrong: In the text the friction comes from the village’s work, thrift, and industry; the do-nothing supplies the “lubricating power” that relieves it.

B.why_wrong: The narrator does contrast the do-nothing with his hardworking neighbors, but he presents him as something every village “must have” because his “lubricating power” keeps society from burning itself out, not as a warning against idleness.

C.why_wrong: The narrator presents the do-nothing as something every village “must have,” and says he takes his ease “in spite of the whole protest of his neighborhood,” so his neighbors do not change him.

sources.what: Internet Archive scan of Stowe, Oldtown Folks (Boston: Fields, Osgood, 1869), chapter IV, The Village Do-Nothing; excerpt copied exactly from the US first edition (neighborhood, not the Low and Tauchnitz neighbourhood), closed em dash after the comma as printed

items.notes: Literary prose, extended figure (steam-power, friction, lubricating). The key needs two steps: industry causes the friction, and the do-nothing is the lubricant. Stowe is a famous author, but this novel is little read and no item uses it (round 1 used Uncle Tom's Cabin, a different subject).

fixes: excerpt checked against three scans of the 1869 Fields, Osgood edition and the British edition on archive.org: exact
hardened: B (works as hard as his neighbors) fell to “won’t work”; now the conventional cautionary reading, partly right (hardworking neighbors, idle man)

band7.why: Planned band 6. Extended figure (steam-power, friction, lubricant) carried into a plain claim in two steps; after the fix all three distractors are partly right (A misplaces the friction, B the conventional cautionary reading, C the neighbors’ protest plus an invented change). Options 14 to 19 words and no irony, so strong band 6, not 7.

items.passage: Along the northwest coast of North America, Indigenous peoples long ago constructed rock walls at the low-tide line of beaches, creating terraces known as clam gardens. Ecologists Amy Groesbeck and Anne Salomon and archaeologist Dana Lepofsky compared 11 such gardens with 10 unmodified beaches on Quadra Island in British Columbia. The gardens contained four times as many butter clams and twice as many littleneck clams, apparently because the walls had flattened each beach’s slope, expanding the stretch of shoreline situated at the tidal height where clams grow and survive best.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Groesbeck and her colleagues found that clam gardens held more clams than unmodified beaches did because the walls protected the clams from predators.
Structures that Indigenous peoples built along the shore appear to have made beaches far more productive for clams by reshaping them.
Rock walls built on beaches across North America show that Indigenous peoples developed many different methods of increasing their supply of shellfish.
The researchers found that Indigenous peoples built clam gardens on gently sloping beaches because such beaches already held the most clams.
items.explanation: The text explains that Indigenous peoples built rock walls that turned beaches into terraced clam gardens, then reports that these gardens held far more clams than unwalled beaches, likely because the walls flattened the beaches and so enlarged the zone where clams do best. The main idea joins the two: the built structures made the beaches much more productive by changing their shape.

A.why_wrong: The text attributes the larger clam numbers to the flatter slope the walls created, which widened the shoreline at the best tidal height, not to protection from predators.

C.why_wrong: The text describes one kind of structure, the clam garden, studied on one island in British Columbia; it says nothing about many different methods of increasing the shellfish supply.

D.why_wrong: The text says the walls themselves flattened the slope of each beach; it does not say the builders chose beaches that were already gentle or rich in clams.

sources.what: ScienceDaily (Simon Fraser University release, March 2014) on Groesbeck, Rowell, Lepofsky and Salomon, PLOS ONE 2014: human-made rock-walled beach terraces called clam gardens built by Aboriginal people; 11 ancient clam gardens and 10 unwalled beaches surveyed on Quadra Island; quadruple the butter clams and twice the littleneck clams; flattening the slope expanded habitat at the intertidal height where clams grow and survive best

items.notes: Archaeology and ecology (Indigenous engineering). Spread main idea: the structure (sentence 1) and its effect with mechanism (sentence 3) must be joined. Key paraphrased away from the passage nouns (structures, reshaping, productive). A gives a wrong mechanism, C stretches one island study to a continent and to many methods, D reverses cause and effect.

band7.why: Planned band 6. Main idea joins structure, finding and mechanism (three statements); key paraphrased (structures, reshaping, productive); distractors TWI (wrong mechanism), BRD, reversed cause, each partly right; options 21 to 23 words against a band-7 main-idea median of 34, and a plain report with no stance word. Strong band 6.

items.passage: Scholars have written extensively about eighteenth-century English novels, frequently assuming that their readership consisted mostly of women. Literary historian Jan Fergus tested that assumption against surviving records kept by booksellers in five market towns in the English Midlands, which document the purchases of more than 3,300 customers between 1744 and 1807. Far from confirming it, the records reveal that men were the principal customers for novels in these towns, even for novels written by women, and that customers generally preferred purchasing fiction to borrowing it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Records studied by Fergus challenge a common belief about these novels’ audience by showing that men in provincial towns were their chief buyers.
Although Fergus found that men bought most of the novels sold in these towns, the records suggest that women bought most novels by women writers.
Fergus’s records leave scholars’ view of the novel’s readership intact, showing only that men were the ones who usually paid for novels.
Records studied by Fergus suggest that scholars misjudged these novels’ readership because they relied on evidence of borrowing rather than of buying.
items.explanation: The text begins with scholars’ assumption that eighteenth-century novels were read mostly by women, then reports that Fergus tested it against booksellers’ records. Rather than confirming it, the records show that men were the main customers for novels in those towns. The main idea is that this evidence overturns the common belief about who bought novels.

B.why_wrong: The records show that men were the principal customers even for novels written by women.

C.recipe: affirms the view the text rejects
C.why_wrong: The text says that, far from confirming the assumption that readers were mostly women, the records show men as the principal customers; it presents the records as overturning that view, not leaving it intact.

D.why_wrong: The records do show that customers preferred buying fiction to borrowing it, but the text never says what evidence scholars relied on or why they assumed most readers were women.

sources.what: Oxford Academic abstract of Jan Fergus, Provincial Readers in Eighteenth-Century England (OUP 2006): archival records of Midland booksellers in five market towns, more than 3,300 customers, 1744 to 1807; contrary to received ideas, men in the provinces were the principal customers for eighteenth-century novels, including those written by women; provincial customers preferred to buy rather than borrow fiction

items.notes: Humanities (book history). View then correction; the key carries both halves (challenge plus finding) and keeps the source's scope (customers in provincial towns, not all readers). The earlier view (readers mostly women) rests on the abstract's contrary to received ideas and its line that women's works would have done better had women been the principal consumers. Every wrong option is two-part and half right: B keeps the men-bought clause, C the men-paid clause, D the buying-over-borrowing clause with an invented cause for the scholars’ error.

fixes: OUP book page blocks fetching; the abstract (five Midland market towns, over 3,300 customers, 1744 to 1807, men the principal customers even for novels by women, preference to buy rather than borrow) confirmed through search
hardened: D (borrowed more than bought) fell to one clause; now keeps the true buying-over-borrowing clause and adds an invented cause for the scholars’ error

band7.why: Planned band 6, after hardening. View then correction signalled by a plain “Far from confirming it”; all three distractors partly right (B a true first clause with a swapped detail, C keeps the buyer finding but affirms the old view, D an invented cause on the true buying clause); options 22 to 25 words. No stance word or litotes, so band 6.

items.passage: Mesophotic coral reefs, which lie 30 to 150 meters below the surface, have been widely regarded as potential refuges for species from increasingly degraded shallow reefs: deep populations, the reasoning goes, could replenish shallow ones. That expectation assumes both that the two kinds of reef share many species and that deep reefs are spared the disturbances affecting shallow ones. Surveying reefs across the Pacific and western Atlantic, Luiz Rocha and colleagues found that most fish species at mesophotic depths live exclusively there and that deep reefs have also sustained damage, for example from storms.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although mesophotic reefs share most of their fish species with shallow reefs, Rocha’s team found that storm damage keeps deep reefs from serving as refuges.
Rocha’s team found that deep reefs escape the harms that affect shallow reefs, though few shallow-reef species could survive at such depths.
Rocha’s team found deep reefs poorly suited to safeguarding shallow-reef species, since the two share fewer species than assumed and both suffer damage.
Because most fish species at mesophotic depths live only there, Rocha’s team concludes that shallow reefs could instead shelter deep-reef species.
items.explanation: The text presents the view that deep reefs could act as refuges for shallow-reef species and notes that the view rests on two assumptions: shared species and protection from harm. Rocha and colleagues’ surveys contradict both, since most deep-reef fish live only at depth and deep reefs have been damaged too. The main idea is that their findings weaken the refuge view on both counts.

A.why_wrong: Damage to deep reefs is reported, but the surveys found that most fish species at mesophotic depths live only there, so the two kinds of reef do not share most species.

B.recipe: affirms an assumption the text rejects (half right)
B.why_wrong: The surveys found that deep reefs, too, have been damaged, so they are not spared the harms shallow reefs face.

D.why_wrong: Species that live only at mesophotic depths are not found on shallow reefs, so the findings give no reason to think shallow reefs could shelter them; the text draws no such conclusion.

sources.what: Pacific Standard on Rocha et al., Science 361:281 (2018): mesophotic reefs long considered potential refuges or lifeboats from which harmed shallow populations could be replenished; surveys across the Pacific and western Atlantic; species overlap, but not much; a majority of reef fish species living at mesophotic depths live only at those depths; mesophotic reefs damaged (buried by sediment after a hurricane); refugia hypothesis not supported. Two assumptions (species overlap, lower susceptibility to impacts) as stated in the paper's abstract

items.notes: Natural science (marine ecology). View then correction with a two-assumption setup; the key must cover both failed assumptions. A and B each keep one true clause and flip the other; D builds a wrong conclusion on the true clause.

fixes: key: “the two share few species” became “the two share fewer species than assumed” (passage and source say most deep-reef fish species live only at depth, overlap “not much”)

band7.why: Planned band 6. Two-assumption setup; the key must answer both; A and B each keep one true clause and flip the other (CON-half), D builds a wrong conclusion on a true clause; options 21 to 25 words. Plain correction without a stance word or aside, so strong band 6.

items.passage: On some glaciers, moss grows into rounded clumps roughly the size of a fist, known as glacier mice, that gradually shift position across the ice. To monitor them, Scott Hotaling, Timothy Bartholomaus, and Sophie Gilbert fitted 30 moss balls on Alaska’s Root Glacier with distinctive beaded bracelets and tracked them over four years. The balls traveled about 2.5 centimeters daily, moving collectively like a herd. Surprisingly, their direction of travel corresponded neither to the glacier’s downhill slope nor to the prevailing wind nor to the direction of the strongest sunlight.
items.stem: According to the text, what was surprising about the movement of the glacier mice?
options: They traveled about 2.5 centimeters per day, slowly shifting their position across the surface of the ice.
Each moss ball followed its own separate route, independent of the routes taken by the others.
They moved steadily downhill, following the slope of the glacier on which they had formed.
The direction in which they moved did not line up with the slope, the wind, or the sun.
items.explanation: The last sentence, which begins with “Surprisingly,” says that the moss balls’ direction of travel matched neither the glacier’s downhill slope, the prevailing wind, nor the direction of the strongest sunlight.

A.why_wrong: The text does report this speed, but it does not present it as surprising; the surprise concerns the direction of travel.

B.why_wrong: The balls moved collectively, like a herd.

C.why_wrong: Their direction of travel did not correspond to the glacier’s downhill slope.

sources.what: Hotaling, Bartholomaus and Gilbert, Rolling stones gather moss: movement and longevity of moss balls on an Alaskan glacier, Polar Biology 2020 (NPS copy): moss balls on the Root Glacier move about 2.5 cm per day in herd-like fashion; surprisingly, the dominant direction does not align with prevailing wind, downslope, or dominant solar radiation; tagged with bead bracelets; fieldwork over four years (2009 to 2012)

items.notes: Natural science (glacier ecology). What-was-surprising frame as in 2.16; distractor A is a true detail that the text does not call surprising.

items.passage: Along the Tollense River in northern Germany, archaeologists have excavated the remains of approximately 140 people, predominantly men between 20 and 40 years old, who died in a battle there around 1250 BCE. Because the excavations have probably recovered only a fraction of the dead, researchers estimate that more than 2,000 combatants may have participated. Chemical analyses of the skeletons suggest that many fighters originated in the south, perhaps in southern Germany or central Europe, a conclusion reinforced by arrowheads and dress pins of central European design found at the site.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one piece of evidence that many of the fighters at Tollense came from outside the region?
options: Most of the people whose remains were found were men between 20 and 40 years old.
Some objects found at the site were made in styles from farther south.
More people took part in the battle than could have lived in the region at the time.
The battle was fought along a river that served as a trade route toward central Europe.
items.explanation: The text says that chemical analyses suggest many fighters came from the south and that this conclusion is “reinforced by arrowheads and dress pins of central European design found at the site.” Objects made in the styles of a region to the south are therefore one piece of evidence.

A.why_wrong: The text does say most of the dead were men aged 20 to 40, but it does not offer their ages as evidence of where they came from.

C.why_wrong: The text estimates that more than 2,000 people may have fought, but it never compares that number with the region’s population or uses it as evidence of the fighters’ origins.

D.why_wrong: The text names the Tollense River as the site of the battle but says nothing about trade routes.

sources.what: Stone Pages archaeology news (from Science) on the Tollense valley battlefield: battlefield dating to 1250 BCE; skeletons of 140 people, mostly men between 20 and 40; probably a fraction of the carnage, more than 2,000 people may have been involved; chemical analyses (strontium, lead, oxygen and carbon isotopes) suggest many came from the south, southern Germany and central Europe, which agrees with Central European-style arrowheads and dress pins

items.notes: Archaeology. One-reason explicit detail; A is a true detail that does not answer the stem; C twists the 2,000 estimate.

items.passage:
The following text is from Charles Dudley Warner’s 1877 book Being a Boy. The narrator recalls driving a team of oxen on a farm when he was a boy, shouting at them and striking them with a long whip just as the adults did.

I think now that it was a cowardly thing to crack the patient old fellows over the face and eyes, and make them wink in their meek manner. If I am ever a boy again on a farm, I shall speak gently to the oxen, and not go screaming round the farm like a crazy man; and I shall not hit them a cruel cut with the lash every few minutes, because it looks big to do so and I cannot think of anything else to do.
items.stem: According to the text, what is one reason the narrator gives for having struck the oxen when he was a boy?
options: Doing so made him look important.
The oxen would not move unless they were struck with the whip.
He wanted to make the oxen wink at him.
The adults on the farm told him to do so.
items.explanation: The narrator says that if he were a boy again he would not hit the oxen every few minutes “because it looks big to do so and I cannot think of anything else to do.” In other words, he struck them partly because it made him seem big and important, like the adults.

B.why_wrong: The narrator calls the oxen “patient old fellows” who wink “in their meek manner”; he never says they refused to move.

C.why_wrong: The oxen’s winking is described as a result of being struck in the face, not as something the narrator wanted.

D.why_wrong: The context says he struck the oxen as the adults did, which means he imitated them; the text never says anyone told him to.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Charles Dudley Warner, Being a Boy (1877), chapter I, Being a Boy; copied exactly, trimmed at sentence boundaries

items.notes: Literary nonfiction (autobiographical sketches). Context line paraphrases the sentences just before the excerpt (he “whacked them with the long lash over the head, just as the big folks did when they drove”). The reason is stated in a because clause, as in 2.10.

items.passage: Analyzing growth rings from nearly 1,400 mostly mature trees in ten cities on several continents, from Berlin to Brisbane, forest scientist Hans Pretzsch and colleagues found that since the 1960s, trees in cities have grown faster than trees in nearby rural areas. The researchers attribute the difference to the urban heat island effect, by which cities retain more heat than outlying rural land. Faster growth, however, is accompanied by accelerated aging, and Pretzsch warns that cities may need to replace aging and dying trees sooner than they once did.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Pretzsch’s team found that city trees outlive rural trees because they grow more quickly.
Trees in rural areas have grown faster than city trees since the 1960s because the countryside is cooler.
Urban warmth seems to have accelerated city trees’ growth, which may also hasten the need to replace them.
Cities in several countries have begun planting more trees in an effort to lower urban temperatures.
items.explanation: The text reports that city trees have grown faster than rural trees since the 1960s, which the researchers attribute to the warmth of cities, and then adds that faster growth brings faster aging, so cities may have to replace their trees sooner. The main idea joins the finding and its consequence.

A.why_wrong: The text says faster growth is accompanied by faster aging, so city trees may need replacing sooner, not that they live longer.

B.why_wrong: The study found that city trees, not rural trees, have grown faster since the 1960s.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about cities planting trees to cool themselves.

sources.what: Technical University of Munich press release (November 2017) on Pretzsch et al., Scientific Reports 7:15403: trees in metropolitan areas have grown faster than rural trees worldwide since the 1960s; heat island effect; ten cities, almost 1,400 mostly mature trees; accelerated aging; city administrations will have to replace aging and dying trees sooner

items.notes: Natural science (urban forestry). Main idea split between finding and consequence, as in medium study reports.

fixes: passage: “Pretzsch warns that cities will need to replace” became “may need to replace” (TUM release: accelerating the life cycle may mean that cities will have to replace trees sooner); explanation and A rationale matched

items.passage: Since the 1960s, researchers have repeatedly asked children in the United States to “draw a scientist.” In the earliest large study, conducted from 1966 to 1977, fewer than 1 percent of nearly 5,000 children depicted a woman. Analyzing 78 such studies involving more than 20,000 children, psychologist David Miller and colleagues determined that in studies from 1985 to 2016, an average of 28 percent of children drew a woman. Around age five, children depicted men and women about equally often, but the tendency to draw men strengthened considerably as children got older.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Most children in the United States now draw female scientists about as often as they draw male scientists, regardless of age.
US children now depict scientists as women far more often than in the past, though their tendency to depict men still grows with age.
Children who draw female scientists are more likely than other children to develop a strong interest in careers in science as they grow older.
Researchers have concluded that asking children to draw a scientist is an unreliable way of learning how children picture scientists.
items.explanation: The text compares the earliest study, in which fewer than 1 percent of children drew a woman, with later studies, in which 28 percent did on average, and then notes that the tendency to draw men grew stronger with age. The main idea combines the large change over time with the remaining pattern by age.

A.why_wrong: On average only 28 percent of children in the later studies drew a woman; drawings were about equal only around age five.

C.why_wrong: The text does not connect children’s drawings with their later interest in science.

D.why_wrong: The researchers used the drawing studies to measure change over time; the text gives no sign that they judged the method unreliable.

sources.what: Northwestern University news (March 2018) on Miller, Nolla, Eagly and Uttal, Child Development 2018: 78 US Draw-A-Scientist studies, more than 20,000 children K-12; 1966 to 1977 study, less than one percent of nearly 5,000 children drew a woman; 1985 to 2016, 28 percent on average; around age 5 roughly equal numbers of male and female scientists, tendency to draw male scientists increased strongly with age

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). Two-part key (change over time plus age pattern); A overstates the 28 percent figure.

items.passage: Aurora Reyes (1908–1985) taught drawing and painting in Mexico’s public schools for nearly four decades. In 1936 she completed Attack on Rural Schoolteachers, a mural in a Mexico City school that depicts violence against teachers in the countryside; she is frequently described as Mexico’s first woman muralist. Between 1960 and 1972, she painted four additional murals in the auditorium of the national teachers’ union, and she also campaigned for causes such as day care for teachers’ children.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Reyes painted her first mural to protest an attack on the school where she taught.
Reyes’s murals became more critical of Mexican society over the course of her long career.
Reyes was better known during her lifetime as a teacher than as a painter of murals.
Much of Reyes’s work as both an artist and an activist was connected to the lives of teachers.
items.explanation: The text says that Reyes was herself a teacher for decades, that her first mural depicts violence against rural teachers, that she later painted murals for the national teachers’ union, and that she campaigned for day care for teachers’ children. Together these details show that teachers were central to her art and activism.

A.why_wrong: The mural depicts violence against teachers in the countryside; the text never says it shows an attack on a school where Reyes taught.

B.why_wrong: The text does not describe how the content or tone of Reyes’s murals changed over time.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how well known Reyes was as a teacher and as a muralist.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Aurora Reyes Flores (1908-1985): described as the first female muralist in Mexico; 1936 mural Atentado a los maestros rurales at the Centro Escolar Revolucion depicting an attack on rural teachers; taught drawing and painting for the Secretariat of Public Education from 1927 to 1964; four murals 1960 to 1972 in the auditorium of the national teachers' union (SNTE); advocated daycare for teachers' children

items.notes: Arts (Mexican muralism). Profile: the key generalizes the examples (teaching, the 1936 mural, the union murals, the campaign) into one theme. The mural title is given in English translation; some sources use the feminine maestras in the Spanish title, so the English title avoids the question.

items.passage:
The following text is from Herbert G. de Lisser’s 1915 novel Susan Proudleigh. Susan lives with her family in a lane in Kingston, Jamaica.

She frequently went for rides on the electric cars, whereas [the others] could only afford such pleasure on Sundays and on public holidays. She carried herself with an air of social superiority which was gall and wormwood to the envious; and often on walking through the lane she had noticed the contemptuous looks of those whom, with greater contempt, she called the common folks and treated with but half-concealed disdain. On the whole, she had rather enjoyed the hostility of these people, for it was in its way a tribute to her own importance.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Susan, who considers herself above her neighbors, takes some satisfaction in their resentment.
Susan is hurt by her neighbors’ hostility and tries to win their friendship by inviting them on her outings.
Susan envies the girls in the lane, who can afford to ride the electric cars more often than she can.
Susan’s neighbors admire the way she carries herself and try to imitate her manners.
items.explanation: The text says that Susan rides the electric cars far more often than her neighbors can, that she carries herself with “an air of social superiority” and treats her neighbors with “half-concealed disdain,” and ends by saying she “rather enjoyed” their hostility as “a tribute to her own importance.” The main idea is that Susan feels superior and takes pleasure in her neighbors’ resentment.

B.why_wrong: Susan treats her neighbors with disdain and enjoys their hostility; nothing suggests she is hurt or wants their friendship.

C.why_wrong: It is Susan who rides the electric cars frequently; the others can afford such rides only on Sundays and holidays.

D.why_wrong: Susan’s manner is “gall and wormwood to the envious,” meaning it embitters them, and they give her contemptuous looks rather than admiring her.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Herbert G. de Lisser, Susan Proudleigh (London: Methuen, first published 1915), chapter I; copied exactly, trimmed at sentence boundaries, with the bracketed gloss [the others] standing for they (whose antecedent, the girls in the lane, is in the omitted sentence before)

items.notes: Literary prose (Jamaican novel, 1915). Excerpt starts at a sentence boundary mid-paragraph; the context line supplies the setting (the lane in Kingston) that the excerpt assumes.

items.passage: At Jiahu, a Neolithic farming settlement in central China occupied from about 7000 to 5700 BCE, archaeologists have recovered six complete flutes fashioned from the wing bones of red-crowned cranes, along with fragments of approximately 30 others. The flutes have between five and eight finger holes. When researchers at the Art Institute of China’s music school played the best-preserved flute, which has seven holes, they found that its notes form a scale remarkably similar to the eight-note scale familiar in Western music.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can be concluded about the flute that the researchers played?
options: It was likely made from a different kind of bone than the other complete flutes found at Jiahu.
It was likely the oldest of the flutes that archaeologists have found at Jiahu.
Its maker likely positioned its holes to produce a deliberately chosen set of notes.
It could likely produce more notes than any of the other flutes found at Jiahu.
items.explanation: The flute’s seven holes produce notes that form a scale remarkably close to a familiar musical scale. A pattern that orderly is unlikely to be an accident, so the person who made the flute probably placed the holes to produce particular notes.

A.why_wrong: The text says the six complete flutes were all fashioned from the wing bones of red-crowned cranes.

B.why_wrong: The text calls this flute the best preserved, not the oldest, and gives no dates for individual flutes.

D.why_wrong: This flute has seven holes, but some of the others have eight, so it cannot be assumed to produce the most notes.

sources.what: ScienceDaily (Brookhaven National Laboratory release, October 1999) on Zhang, Harbottle, Wang and Kong, Nature 401:366: six intact flutes 7,000 to 9,000 years old and fragments of about 30 others from Jiahu, made from the ulnae (wing bones) of the red-crowned crane, five to eight holes; the best-preserved flute played and tonally analyzed at the Music School of the Art Institute of China; its seven holes correspond to a carefully selected tone scale remarkably similar to the Western eight-note scale

items.notes: Archaeology and music. Premises: seven holes; the notes form an orderly, familiar scale. Conclusion (the release's own word: carefully selected): the hole positions were chosen. Occupation dates (7000 to 5700 BC) from the Nature abstract.

items.passage: Judith Leyster (1609–1660) became a member of the painters’ guild of Haarlem in the Netherlands in 1633, and within two years she had taken on three apprentices. After her death, however, her paintings were largely forgotten or attributed to other artists, including Frans Hals, a considerably more celebrated Haarlem painter. Her work regained wide recognition only in 1893, when a painting that the Louvre had purchased as a Hals was discovered to bear her monogram concealed beneath a fraudulent Hals signature.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Leyster trained Frans Hals as one of her apprentices, which explains why their paintings were so often confused with each other.
Leyster succeeded in her own time, but because much of her work was credited to others, she was overlooked for centuries.
Leyster’s paintings were rediscovered in 1893, when the Louvre began searching for works by the women of the Haarlem guild.
Leyster signed some of her paintings with Hals’s name so that collectors would pay more for them than they would for her own work.
items.explanation: The text first establishes that Leyster succeeded in her lifetime (guild membership, apprentices), then explains that after her death her paintings were forgotten or attributed to other artists until 1893. The main idea is that a painter recognized in her day went unrecognized for a long time because her work was credited to others.

A.why_wrong: The text says Leyster took on three apprentices but never says Hals was one of them.

C.why_wrong: The Louvre had bought the painting believing it was by Hals; her monogram was found on it, and nothing suggests the museum was searching for works by women.

D.why_wrong: The painting bore her own monogram concealed beneath a signature the text calls fraudulent; nothing indicates that Leyster added Hals’s name.

sources.what: New World Encyclopedia, Judith Leyster (1609-1660): member of the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke by 1633; within two years of entering the guild she had three male apprentices; works mostly forgotten or falsely attributed to other artists until 1893, when the Louvre bought what it thought was a Frans Hals painting and her monogram was found hidden under a false Frans Hals signature

items.notes: Arts (Dutch painting, attribution history). View then correction at medium: reputation in her lifetime, then centuries of misattribution, then rediscovery.

items.passage: Painted lady butterflies are among the most widespread butterflies on Earth, and each spring vast numbers of them arrive in Europe to breed. But where do the butterflies go when they leave Europe in the autumn? In 2014, biologists Gerard Talavera and Roger Vila observed painted ladies migrating south through Chad and breeding abundantly in Benin and Ethiopia. Meanwhile, a team led by Constantí Stefanescu analyzed hydrogen in the wings of painted ladies captured south of the Sahara, which reflects where each butterfly developed as a caterpillar, and determined that those butterflies had originated in Europe.
items.stem: Which question does the text most directly attempt to answer?
options: Why do painted lady butterflies leave Europe in the autumn?
How long does a painted lady live once it reaches Africa?
How do painted ladies find their way across the Sahara?
Where do painted lady butterflies go after leaving Europe in the autumn?
items.explanation: The text asks “where do the butterflies go when they leave Europe in the autumn?” and then answers it: fieldwork found painted ladies migrating south and breeding in sub-Saharan Africa, and wing analyses showed that butterflies captured there had originated in Europe.

A.recipe: plausible but unsupported (question not taken up)
A.why_wrong: The text asks and answers where the butterflies go after they leave Europe, not why they leave.

B.recipe: plausible but unsupported (question not taken up)
B.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how long the butterflies live.

C.recipe: plausible but unsupported (question not taken up)
C.why_wrong: The text shows that butterflies from Europe reached lands south of the Sahara but says nothing about how they navigate.

sources.what: Science News (2016) on Talavera and Vila, Biological Journal of the Linnean Society 2016, and Stefanescu et al., Biology Letters 2016: the route of painted ladies between Europe and Africa largely unknown; in 2014 Talavera and Vila visited Benin, Chad, Ethiopia and Senegal, found butterflies moving south through Chad and dense breeding aggregations in Benin and Ethiopia; Stefanescu's team analyzed hydrogen isotopes in wings, which reflect where the butterflies lived as larvae; those in sub-Saharan Africa had started in Europe

items.notes: Natural science (insect migration). Explicit question plus answer, as in 2.20; the three distractors are on-topic questions the text never answers, one of them (C) built on the crossing the text does mention.

fixes: source note: the Stefanescu hydrogen-isotope study is in Biology Letters (as the Science News page says), not Ecography

items.passage: In fourteenth-century England, most ale was brewed by women, who were known as brewsters. Brewing was typically part of a woman’s household work, and when she produced more ale than her family required, she might sell the surplus to provide income for the household. In her book Ale, Beer, and Brewsters in England, historian Judith Bennett describes how this situation changed between 1300 and 1600, as brewing shifted from small household production to large commercial breweries that employed many workers and were managed by men.
items.stem: According to the text, why did some women in fourteenth-century England sell ale?
options: They wanted to provide income for their households.
They were competing with large breweries run by men.
They needed money to buy equipment for making beer.
They had been hired by breweries to sell ale in town.
items.explanation: The text says that when a woman made more ale than her family needed, “she might sell the surplus to provide income for the household.”

B.why_wrong: Large breweries run by men belong to the later change the text describes, between 1300 and 1600, not to the reason fourteenth-century women sold ale.

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions buying brewing equipment.

D.why_wrong: The text describes brewing as part of a woman’s own household work, not as a job for a brewery.

sources.what: Times Higher Education review of Judith M. Bennett, Ale, Beer, and Brewsters in England: Women's Work in a Changing World, 1300-1600 (OUP 1996): in 14th-century England most brewing of ale was done by women, the brewsters, as part of domestic work; surpluses might be sold to provide income for the household; shift from small domestic production to larger breweries employing many people, managed by men by 1600

items.notes: History (medieval economy and women's work). Easy explicit detail; the key echoes the target sentence, as easy keys do.

items.passage: In colonies of Indian jumping ants, the death of the queen triggers a competition among the workers. The few winners, called gamergates, assume the queen’s role of laying eggs, and their brains shrink by about 19 percent, probably conserving energy for egg production. Biologist Clint Penick and his colleagues separated some gamergates from their colonies for several weeks. Those ants resumed behaving like ordinary workers, and their brains returned to their original size.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened to the gamergates that the researchers separated from their colonies?
options: They began laying more eggs than they had before.
Their brains shrank by about 19 percent.
They acted like workers again, and their brains regrew.
They fought other workers to take over the queen’s role.
items.explanation: The text says that the separated gamergates “resumed behaving like ordinary workers, and their brains returned to their original size.”

A.why_wrong: The separated ants resumed behaving like ordinary workers rather than laying more eggs.

B.why_wrong: Brains shrink by about 19 percent when workers become gamergates; the separated ants’ brains returned to their original size.

D.why_wrong: The competition among workers happens when a queen dies; the text does not say the separated ants fought.

sources.what: NPR story (via GPB, April 2021) on Penick et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B 2021: when the queen dies a dominance tournament begins; winners called gamergates take on egg laying; their brains shrink by 19% on average, likely saving energy for egg production; gamergates removed from their colonies for a few weeks returned to being workers with their brains regrown

items.notes: Natural science (insect behavior and neurobiology). B is a true detail from the passage that does not answer the stem.

items.passage:
The following text is from Lucy Larcom’s 1889 memoir A New England Girlhood. After the death of the narrator’s father, her mother was left to care for eight children with very little money.

I knew that she believed in God, and in the promises of the Bible, and yet she seemed sometimes to forget everything but her troubles and her helplessness. I felt almost like preaching to her, but I was too small a child to do that, I well knew; so I did the next best thing I could think of—I sang hymns as if singing to myself, while I meant them for her.
items.stem: According to the text, why does the narrator sing hymns?
options: She wants to show her mother how many hymns she has learned.
She hopes to help her mother, who is weighed down by her troubles.
She is practicing so that she can preach to her mother later.
Her mother has asked her to sing while the family works.
items.explanation: The narrator says that her mother “seemed sometimes to forget everything but her troubles,” and that, being too young to preach to her, she “sang hymns as if singing to myself, while I meant them for her.” She sings to help her troubled mother.

A.why_wrong: The narrator never says she wants to show off the hymns she knows; she sings them for her mother’s sake.

C.why_wrong: The narrator says she was too small to preach and sang instead; she does not say she is practicing for preaching later.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says that her mother asked her to sing.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Lucy Larcom, A New England Girlhood, Outlined from Memory (1889; preface dated October 1889), chapter VII, Beginning to Work; copied exactly, the double hyphen of the e-text set as a closed em dash

items.notes: Literary nonfiction (memoir). Context line paraphrases the preceding paragraph (her mother left with eight children and no property except the house and a small strip of land).

items.passage: Plastic bags and wrappers are frequently discarded after a single use, and much of this waste accumulates in landfills or along roadsides. Rajagopalan Vasudevan, a chemistry professor in Madurai, India, devised a practical use for such waste. He shredded discarded plastic and blended it with bitumen, the sticky black material that binds road surfaces together. Roads constructed with his method have proved durable and resistant to damage from heavy rainfall, and the technique is now widely used in rural India.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Vasudevan showed that plastic can completely replace bitumen in the surfaces of roads.
Vasudevan found a way to use plastic waste in building roads that hold up well.
Most of the plastic waste in India now goes into new roads instead of into landfills.
Roads in rural India are more often damaged by heavy rain than roads in cities are.
items.explanation: The text describes the problem of discarded plastic, explains that Vasudevan blended shredded plastic with bitumen to build roads, and reports that those roads are durable and resist damage from rainfall. The main idea is that he found a way to turn plastic waste into a useful ingredient for sturdy roads.

A.why_wrong: Vasudevan blended plastic with bitumen; the text does not say the plastic replaces bitumen.

C.why_wrong: The text says the technique is widely used in rural India, not that most of India’s plastic waste goes into roads.

D.why_wrong: The text never compares rain damage on rural and city roads.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Rajagopalan Vasudevan: professor at Thiagarajar College of Engineering (Madurai); idea of shredding plastic waste and mixing it with bitumen for road construction; roads more durable and very cost-effective, with greater resistance to damage caused by heavy rains; method widely used to construct roads in rural India; Padma Shri 2018

items.notes: Technology and engineering. Profile-style study report at easy level; governing claim split between the method and its result.

items.passage: Many people avoid repeating an experience, such as watching a movie a second time, because they expect it to be less enjoyable than it was originally. Psychologist Ed O’Brien tested that expectation. Participants visited a museum exhibit, watched a movie, or played a video game. Some then predicted how much they would enjoy repeating the activity immediately, while others actually repeated it. Those who repeated the activity enjoyed it more than the predictions indicated, apparently because they noticed details they had previously missed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: People enjoy watching a movie a second time more than they enjoy visiting a museum exhibit again.
Doing something for the second time is usually more enjoyable than doing it for the first time.
Researchers found that people who play video games repeat activities more often than other people do.
Research suggests that people underestimate how much they will enjoy repeating an experience.
items.explanation: The text explains that people expect repeated experiences to be less enjoyable, then reports that in O’Brien’s study those who actually repeated an activity enjoyed it more than others had predicted. The main idea is that people tend to underestimate the enjoyment of repeating an experience.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares enjoyment of repeated movies with repeated museum visits.

B.why_wrong: The text says repeaters enjoyed the activity more than predicted, not more than the first time.

C.why_wrong: Playing a video game was one of the activities in the study; the text says nothing about video game players repeating activities more often.

sources.what: Chicago Booth Review on O'Brien, Enjoy It Again: Repeat Experiences Are Less Repetitive Than People Think (JPSP 2019): participants experienced a museum exhibit, a movie, or a video game once; predictors overestimated how much repeating would reduce enjoyment; repeat experiences feel fresh because people discover new aspects

items.notes: Social science (psychology). Easy study report; governing claim in the last sentence.

fixes: passage: “often because they noticed” became “apparently because they noticed” (Chicago Booth Review: two experiments suggest repeats feel fresh because people discover new aspects)

items.passage:
The following text is from George and Weedon Grossmith’s 1892 novel The Diary of a Nobody. Carrie is the narrator’s wife.

APRIL 30.—Perfectly astounded at receiving an invitation for Carrie and myself from the Lord and Lady Mayoress to the Mansion House, to “meet the Representatives of Trades and Commerce.” My heart beat like that of a schoolboy’s. Carrie and I read the invitation over two or three times. I could scarcely eat my breakfast. I said—and I felt it from the bottom of my heart,—“Carrie darling, I was a proud man when I led you down the aisle of the church on our wedding-day; that pride will be equalled, if not surpassed, when I lead my dear, pretty wife up to the Lord and Lady Mayoress at the Mansion House.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator worries that his wife will feel out of place among the important guests at the Mansion House.
The narrator is surprised that his wife does not share his excitement about the invitation.
The narrator is thrilled and proud to have been invited to an important event with his wife.
The narrator remembers his wedding day and wishes that he could live it over again.
items.explanation: The narrator is “perfectly astounded” by the invitation, his heart beats “like that of a schoolboy’s,” he can “scarcely eat” his breakfast, and he says his pride at taking his wife to the Mansion House will equal or surpass his pride on his wedding day. He is thrilled and proud.

A.why_wrong: The narrator calls his wife his “dear, pretty wife” and looks forward to leading her up to the Lord and Lady Mayoress; he expresses no worry about her.

B.why_wrong: Carrie reads the invitation over two or three times with him, so she shares his interest; nothing suggests she is unexcited.

D.why_wrong: The narrator mentions his wedding day only to compare his pride then with the pride he expects to feel at the Mansion House.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of George and Weedon Grossmith, The Diary of a Nobody (1892, J. W. Arrowsmith), chapter IV, entry for April 30; copied exactly (double spaces after periods reduced to one), trimmed at a sentence boundary

items.notes: Literary prose (comic diary novel). Clear emotional state for an easy main-idea item; the diary heading and the closed em dashes are kept as printed.

items.passage: Toyo Miyatake (1895–1979) operated a photography studio in Los Angeles. In 1942, during World War II, he and his family were among the thousands of Japanese Americans forcibly confined at the Manzanar incarceration camp in California, where cameras were prohibited. Miyatake smuggled in a camera lens, had a camera body constructed from wood, and secretly photographed daily life in the camp. Eventually the camp’s director permitted him to work openly, and Miyatake became the camp’s official photographer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Miyatake found ways to keep working as a photographer even while he was incarcerated.
Miyatake was the only Japanese American allowed to bring a camera into Manzanar.
Miyatake closed his Los Angeles studio so that he could take pictures of life in the camps.
Miyatake’s photographs of Manzanar became famous after the camp’s director found them.
items.explanation: The text explains that cameras were prohibited at Manzanar, yet Miyatake smuggled in a lens, had a camera built, photographed camp life in secret, and later became the camp’s official photographer. The main idea is that he kept working as a photographer despite his incarceration.

B.why_wrong: Cameras were prohibited in the camp; Miyatake smuggled in a lens rather than being allowed to bring a camera.

C.why_wrong: Miyatake was forcibly confined in the camp; the text does not say he closed his studio by choice in order to photograph the camps.

D.why_wrong: The text says the director eventually permitted Miyatake to work openly; it says nothing about the director finding the photographs or about their fame.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Toyo Miyatake (1895-1979): photo studio in Los Angeles; incarcerated at Manzanar with his wife and four children; smuggled a camera lens into the camp and had a camera body constructed from wood; secretly took photographs of the camp; Manzanar director Ralph Merritt later made him the official camp photographer

items.notes: Arts and history (photography, Japanese American incarceration). Profile at easy level; the key generalizes the examples.
